memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "Next they made the courtyard. The south side was a hundred cubits long and had curtains of finely twisted linen, with twenty posts and twenty bronze bases, and with silver hooks and bands on the posts. The north side was also a hundred cubits long and had twenty posts and twenty bronze bases, with silver hooks and bands on the posts." - Exod 38:9-11 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
A hundred cubits of linen curtain on each side — roughly forty-five metres. The courtyard had a clear, visible boundary.

Anyone in the camp could see where the sacred space began and where it ended. There was no confusion about it.

Boundaries have a poor reputation in our time. They sound restrictive, unwelcoming, narrow. But consider what this boundary actually did. It made the space identifiable. Without it, the tabernacle would have simply blurred into the surrounding camp, and nothing would have been set apart at all.

God's people have always needed this. Not walls of hostility toward outsiders — the courtyard had a wide entrance, as we will see — but a clear sense of what belongs to God and what does not.

Paul told the Corinthians they were God's temple and urged them not to be yoked together with unbelievers in ways that compromised that (2 Cor 6:14-16). Not withdrawal from people; distinction in allegiance.

Practically, this means having some settled lines in your life decided in advance. What you will and will not do. What you will not watch, say, or participate in. Decisions made calmly beforehand are far easier to keep than decisions made under pressure.

What are your linen curtains?

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. What boundaries have you actually settled in advance?
2. Where has a blurred line cost you something?
3. How do you stay distinct without becoming unwelcoming?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord, help me draw clear lines in my life, and to hold them with a warm heart toward everyone outside them. Amen.
